On April 10, 2025, Freedom for Eurasia, the Ukrainian Fund of International Volunteers, and the banned Islamic Renaissance Party (IRPT), represented by French lawyer Nicolas Ligneul, filed an Article 15 communication with the ICC. The filing organizations say it documents killings, torture, sexual violence, enforced disappearances, and forced exile between 2002 and 2024, and asks prosecutors to examine the responsibility of senior officials, including President Emomali Rahmon. Their chosen start date for communication is the day the ICC statute took effect in Tajikistan.
A communication does not mean a case has been opened; the Office of the Prosecutor has not announced an investigation. Even if it did, exiting the ICC wouldn’t be a clean escape for Tajikistan. Withdrawal does not cancel obligations incurred while a party, and it does not automatically strip the court of jurisdiction over alleged crimes committed before the exit date. An exit would mainly limit exposure for conduct after that – which matters to the Tajik leadership given that succession from father to son is widely expected, and rumored to require Putin’s approval.
The international cost of leaving the ICC looks lower than it did even a year ago. Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger notified withdrawal in June, Venezuela and Chad in July; none of those states will be out before mid-2027. Hungary rescinded its notification on May 29, days before it was due to take effect. The EU criticized Tajikistan’s failure to arrest Putin but initialed an Enhanced Partnership and Cooperation Agreement (EPCA) with Dushanbe in July 2025 anyway and aims to sign it this year. Quitting the ICC breaches no trade condition – the Rome Statute is not among the conventions the EU’s preference schemes require – but it is a poor advertisement for an agreement whose selling point is shared values.
On September 16, Tajikistan’s lower house of parliament considered a draft resolution on withdrawing from the International Criminal Court (ICC) at an extraordinary session. The parliamentary press service reported only that “corresponding decisions were taken,” naming neither the sponsor nor the rationale and saying nothing about a plenary vote.
The domestic steps required for the withdrawal under Tajik law have not been made public. Internationally, Article 127 of the Rome Statute requires written notification to the U.N. secretary general, with withdrawal taking effect one year later; the U.N. treaty database still lists Tajikistan as a state party.
articles.summary: The move comes a year after Tajikistan’s refusal to arrest Russian President Vladimir Putin brought a formal rebuke from The Hague.

articles.title: Why Is Lee Jae-myung’s Approval Rating Dropping?
articles.full_text:
Four developments, from the fading Yoon effect to failed nominations, help explain a slide to 37 percent that the South Korean president attributes to his own shortcomings.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung blamed his own shortcomings for a steep loss of public support. His approval rating fell to 37 percent in a Gallup Korea poll released that morning, the lowest level since he took office in June 2025.
At a standing news conference at the presidential Blue House on September 18, Lee described the decline as puzzling at first. 
“In the end, I came to think that all of it, taken together, was because of my own shortcomings,” Lee said. And in opening remarks, he noted that he had been flustered by the disappointment that followed the June 3 local elections.
However, the slide began earlier. Support for Lee – who took office in June 2025 – had hovered near 60 percent for months before it started falling in mid-May. 
Among respondents who disapprove of him, 20 percent cited housing policy and 16 percent cited personnel appointments in the latest survey.
Aside from specific events, four border trends help explain the slide of the president’s approval ratings.
The first is the fading of the Yoon Suk-yeol effect. Lee won the presidency in a special election following the impeachment of Yoon, who had illegitimately declared martial law in December 2024. For months the contrast with his predecessor helped sustain Lee’s ratings. That contrast has weakened over time. Yoon was sentenced to life in prison in February for leading an insurrection. His wife, Kim Keon-hee, had her sentence increased to four years on appeal in April. Although their sentences will likely need to be confirmed in the Supreme Court, which will take years, the question for voters appears to have shifted from who should be punished to who is fixing daily life. It has already been more than 21 months after the martial law declaration and many South Koreans have moved on.
The second trend is a gap between the image of a hands-on executive Lee cultivated as a mayor and governor and the delegator he now describes. On Friday, he said he has neither the time nor the ability to micromanage everything. Lee has told staff to refrain from involvement in routine ministry business. His principle is to give authority and hold people firmly accountable.
However, the rollout of single-stock leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs) shows the risk of this approach. These stock products have hurt retail investors, and South Koreans want an explanation. Former Presidential Policy Chief Kim Yong-beom said in January that he had instructed regulators to review the products. The ETFs went on sale on May 27, days before the local elections. Regulators tightened the rules on July 16 and again on July 29 as losses mounted. The policy chief resigned on September 1, and the Blue House did not give a reason. 
In his press conference on September 18, Lee said he did not yet know the details of how the products were approved, although he “received a report at the time,” he recalled. Lee conceded that it seems true that there were shortcomings. In such comments, voters who backed him for getting things done may see a president who owns the results but not the process. 
Housing is another area where Lee has failed to convince voters he is solving the problem. It is the most cited reason for disapproval in the Gallup Korea polling. Lee, for his part, pointed out that prices in outlying areas are still climbing even as those in wealthy Gangnam, the emblematic district for wealth in Seoul, soften.
The third problem is communication. Scrutiny of a president tends to sharpen in the second year, and the local elections gave critics an opening. The ruling Democratic Party won 12 of 16 mayoral and gubernatorial races but lost Seoul, where Lee had publicly backed the DP’s candidate, Chong Won-o. During his press conference commemorating his first year in the presidency on June 8, Lee said that losing places the party should have won made the result “at the least, not a success.” 
Asked how he would talk to the public about housing, specifically, Lee didn’t seem to have an answer. He said on Friday that he would study a variety of methods and invited suggestions. Lee closed by promising to communicate more, listen more and respect more.
However, voters have other questions for him. The Kospi closed on September 18 about 24 percent below its June 22 peak. The relationship with Washington keeps shifting. North Korea has stopped answering Seoul. On each of those, voters appear to be waiting to hear from the president himself.
U.S. President Donald Trump has pressed Seoul for help in the U.S. war with Iran, especially in reopening the Strait of Hormuz. On March 14, two weeks after beginning strikes against Iran, Trump urged South Korea and four other countries to send warships to the strait. 
On August 16, he wrote on Truth Social that he had asked Lee whether South Korea would join “the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran.” South Korea replied, according to Trump, “No thanks!” In the same post, he ordered the Pentagon to substantially reduce joint exercises with South Korea.
During his press conference, Lee ruled out sending troops to take part in the Iran-U.S. war. “There will be no dispatch of troops that involves or intervenes in the war,” he said. 
Still, he noted that a naval unit is already stationed near the Strait of Hormuz. And the Blue House said on Saturday that Lee had not rejected the request from Trump for cooperation on Middle East issues. So South Koreans may be left feeling uncertain as to what the Lee administration will actually do in the Middle East.
On North Korea, Lee said Pyongyang “is clearly refusing to communicate with South Korea.” He added that Trump wants dialogue with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and that Seoul is coordinating in advance to make talks possible. He dismissed concerns that South Korea could be sidelined.
The fourth problem for Lee, as mentioned above, is personnel. Five ministerial appointments have been forced to withdraw – starting just a month after Lee took office. His education minister pick, Lee Jin-sook, withdrew in July 2025 amid plagiarism allegations. More recently, Yong Hye-in, a two-time lawmaker in the Basic Income Party who was nominated as gender equality minister, withdrew from consideration on September 13. 
In his press conference on Friday, Lee promised a review of how nominees are vetted. “I plan to re-examine the personnel system now,” Lee said, though he could not promise that problems would never recur.
Kim Seung-won, Lee’s justice minister appointee who was attracted critical reporting from the press and belligerence from opposition lawmakers, withdrew the next morning. He was the fifth Lee nominee to fall through since he took office.
When Lee had announced a reshuffle on August 30, his chief of staff, Kang Hoon-sik, said competence was the sole criterion. Nonetheless, South Koreans continued to find flaws with his choices. In a Gallup Korea poll released September 11, 61 percent of respondents called Yong unfit and 43 percent said the same of Kim Seung-won. 
In order to take responsibility for the downward slide in Lee’s approval ratings and the recent series of missteps the Blue House has taken, Kang offered to resign on September 21. According to local media reports, Lee said he has not made any decisions on whether to accept his resignation.

articles.title: Why Sri Lanka’s Ruling NPP Has Not Abolished the Executive Presidency Yet
articles.full_text:
It is prioritizing economic recovery and establishing accountability of powerful people for past crimes to build the mass support needed to pursue constitutional reform.
Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake.
Civil society critics of Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake and the National People’s Power (NPP) government are again asking why they haven’t launched a constitutional reform process to abolish the executive presidency.
A number of governments, starting with the Chandrika Bandaranaike administration (1994-2005), had promised to abolish the executive presidency introduced by the J.R. Jayawardene administration in the late 1970s. The main argument against the executive presidency is that it concentrates too much power in one individual, the president, which is bad for democratic processes.
The Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP), the main component of the NPP, has been critical of the executive presidency for decades.
It has been two years since the NPP came to power and its critics regard the delay in constitutional reform as a retreat from the mandate that brought Dissanayake and the NPP to power. However, that interpretation gives disproportionate weight to one electoral promise while ignoring many others. The NPP’s actions in the past two years also show that it is focused on accomplishing reforms that have more visible outcomes.
Dissanayake and the NPP’s appeal rested mainly on its reputation for honesty and its distance from the political establishment that ruled the nation since its independence. These rulers were culpable for Sri Lanka’s economic collapse and 2022 debt default, a fact that has been affirmed even by the country’s Supreme Court. Voters who lost faith in the established parties following the economic trauma of 2022 believed that Dissanayake and his party could form a government that would use public resources responsibly and hold powerful people accountable.
The NPP sought a mandate that extended well beyond constitutional reform. Those who voted for the NPP expected economic recovery and action against corruption that previous governments had allowed to flourish. Horu allamu (Let’s punish the crooks) was the rallying cry of the 2024 elections, and the arrests of several powerful politicians have been welcomed with great public enthusiasm.
The government is also implementing an island-wide anti-drug campaign, the Clean Sri Lanka Project, and a digitization drive. The NPP has prioritized these initiatives that enhance the quality of life of the people and satisfy the public demand to prosecute the corrupt. The resources the NPP has at its disposal are limited, and the government believes that it has pick battles that it can win while governing a country still recovering from economic collapse and exposed to fresh external shocks.
The lesson the NPP learned from the disastrous performance of the Yahapalanaya (good governance) government (2014-2019) was that delivering on promises that produce immediate results should be prioritized.
The Yahapalanaya government established a Constitutional Assembly and steering committee in 2016. Subcommittees examined specific subjects, and an interim report was published in 2017. These committees produced proposals and debate, but these did not result in a new constitution. Besides, the government failed to deliver on its other promises, especially on investigating and punishing the Rajapaksas for their alleged financial crimes. This led to public disillusionment, which allowed the Rajapaksas to return to power in 2019.
Sri Lanka’s economy grew by 5 percent in 2025, and by 4.2 percent in the second quarter of 2026. However, the country is vulnerable to external shocks and the IMF has warned that the war in West Asia has significantly worsened the economic outlook.
Sri Lanka imports all its fossil fuels and LNG and most of its fertilizer. Higher energy costs would threaten household budgets and the foreign exchange reserves. Disruption of fertilizer supplies puts pressure on agriculture. China’s restrictions on fertilizer exports and Russia’s temporary suspension of ammonium nitrate exports earlier this year are worrying developments. These are immediate problems for a government determined to prevent another economic collapse that might spell the doom of the NPP.
Judicial reforms are a cornerstone in the NPP’s drive to prosecute corrupt politicians. The proposed Twenty-Second Amendment addresses retirement ages for superior court judges and the tenure of the chief justice, which the government believes is vital to expedite high-profile cases. The NPP believes that if senior judges who have handled these cases retire when verdicts are close, that would delay punishment.
One of the tactics of corrupt politicians is to delay cases against them as much as possible, hoping that the momentum behind the investigations would wane. The government faces stiff opposition in implementing its initiatives, and dealing with these has taken up its time and resources.
Abolishing the executive presidency is not an easy task. Provincial councils are connected to presidential authority through provisions introduced by the Thirteenth Amendment. Under Article 154B, the president appoints provincial governors, who exercise provincial executive power within a framework that includes the advice of provincial ministers and specified discretionary functions.
Article 154F subjects governors’ exercise of discretion to presidential directions. Article 154L authorizes presidential intervention when provincial administration cannot function constitutionally, subject to prescribed procedures. These provisions make the presidency an integral part of the relationship between the center and the provinces. The relevant powers are detailed in Chapter XVIIA of the Constitution.
Provincial councils could continue under a parliamentary system. But reformers will have to agree on who appoints governors and controls the powers currently exercised by the president. Transferring those powers wholesale to a prime minister could preserve central control and giving provinces greater autonomy would require agreement on safeguards and mechanisms for resolving disputes. Apart from these technicalities, the thirteenth amendment and devolving power to the provinces are controversial topics in Sri Lanka.
Coming up with a solution to this aspect of dissolving the executive alone would consume colossal amounts of the government’s time, and it seems that the NPP government has decided it doesn’t want to at the present time.
Critics are nevertheless right to insist the NPP must not forget its pledge to abolish the executive presidency. The NPP has 159 seats in the 225-seat parliament, which would allow it to pass any constitutional amendment it wants. This was how new constitutions were passed in the past by governments that had the necessary numbers, for example in 1972 and 1978.
The problem with the NPP government is that it continues to give vague assurances of constitutional reforms, while it is obvious that these reforms are not a priority for them right now. It would make more sense for the government to tell the public the place constitutional reform occupies in its program.  Being honest with what its priorities are and why would provide clarity to the people and those who are invested in certain aspects of the reform process.
On the other hand, NPP critics must recognize that credibility earned through effective administration creates an opportunity for constitutional reform. If economic recovery becomes permanent and justice is served for past crimes by powerful people, the NPP will be better placed to create and implement a new constitution that has the support of most Sri Lankans.
The NPP should ultimately be judged across the mandate it sought. Voters expected a government capable of repairing public institutions and protecting the country from another economic disaster.
Abolition of the presidency remains an important task. But the absence of a constitutional commission does not establish that the government has abandoned meaningful reform. Its critics should examine why the NPP has chosen to prioritize some promises over others and distinguish a government that postpones reform to preserve its privileges from one that sequences difficult commitments to make them achievable.

articles.title: Chinese Data Centers Will Shape ASEAN’s AI Norms
articles.full_text:
Southeast Asian governments’ reliance on foreign capital, expertise, and capacity could leave them vulnerable over the longer term.
The official launch ceremony for the China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Industry Innovation Center in Beijing, China, May 24, 2026.
In June, Alibaba Cloud opened two data centers in Johor, bringing the number of Alibaba facilities in Malaysia to a total of five–its largest data center presence in Southeast Asia. The opening came four months after ASEAN endorsed a Malaysia-led framework governing cross-border cloud computing, which set regional principles for data protection, regulatory access, and cross-border data hosting.
Yet even as Malaysia helps write ASEAN’s cloud rules, the region’s growing reliance on Chinese infrastructure may embed norms shaped by Chinese law and comparatively weak or opaque safeguards against cyber misuse, regardless of the principles expressed in member state policies. It may also favor Chinese models whose developers disclose less about such safeguards, even as Beijing tightly controls politically sensitive content in Chinese-developed models. ASEAN governments should thus treat data center investment as a form of AI governance and norms diffusion, rather than a matter primarily or solely of industrial policy.
Only a few companies can provide data centers, computing capacity, and complete cloud and AI systems at the required scale. Cloud providers can influence technical practices beyond their own facilities. Firms and agencies building on their platforms must make their systems compatible with the providers’ services and meet requirements for access, configuration, and security. Because so many digital services depend on data centers, the technical specifications and operating practices adopted in Chinese-built or Chinese-operated facilities will shape the services that run on them.
These facilities are therefore an early place to examine whether Chinese involvement is translating into broader influence over technical standards and operational norms. Dependency through platform lock-in allows this influence to develop and become durable within systems and creates a risk that the government could lose practical control over its use of those systems. Once government agencies and highly regulated industries build services around one provider, implementing different privacy or security standards would often require redesigning entire ecosystems, retraining workers, and shouldering substantial migration costs.
Chinese cloud providers have expanded their footprint in Malaysia and Indonesia through partnerships with governments and businesses to embed their cloud services into the core infrastructure of the digital economy. Even when operating abroad, Chinese cloud providers must comply with China’s Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law, and National Intelligence Law. These laws create pathways for the Chinese government to compel access to data deemed relevant to national security, not unlike the USA PATRIOT Act, CLOUD Act, and FISA 702. Those same obligations helped U.S. prosecutors build their case against Chinese intelligence officer Xu Yanjun. Under a warrant issued in December 2017, Apple provided the FBI with his iCloud data, which supported his arrest in Belgium and extradition to the U.S. the following year. ASEAN governments are likely aware that using Chinese infrastructure carries risks to personal data, as does using U.S. infrastructure.
In addition to building AI infrastructure in Malaysia, Alibaba is also beginning to train people in how to use it. In 2025, Selangor state recognized Alibaba Cloud as a provider under its Multi Cloud Services initiative. The company now offers training in its proprietary AI Toolkit and certification courses to government agencies, educators, students, and local communities. It has also partnered with the Malaysia Digital Economy Corporation – the government agency under the Ministry of Digital leading the Malaysian economy’s technological transformation  – to train small and medium-sized enterprises in adopting cloud computing and AI.
In Indonesia, Huawei has developed similar relationships, such as partnering with the National Cyber and Crypto Agency and the Institut Teknologi Del, establishing a Huawei Academy, and providing digital literacy and cybersecurity training to the Indonesian Air Force. Huawei describes these programs as a means of sharing cybersecurity “best practices” built on its tools and expertise. Through training and socialization, such practices can become the foundation of professional norms.
Sharing best practices and developing norms is not inherently malicious. But these practices are taking root in a region where digital rules and enforcement remain uneven, while intensifying U.S.-China AI competition is making ASEAN countries an increasing focus of U.S. law enforcement action. In Indonesia, a 2024 study found that vague definitions, limited enforcement, and inadequate provisions for AI or big data weakened implementation of the country’s 2022 data protection law. Although the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation has influenced regional privacy laws, it has not produced uniform standards or enforcement, leaving room for providers’ practices to become defaults. Malaysia’s proposed safeguards may help, but businesses and agencies dependent on one provider may find switching too costly and accommodate practices at odds with domestic privacy goals.
This Chinese infrastructure buildout may also directly support advanced Chinese AI development. The Financial Times reported in November 2025 that Alibaba and ByteDance were training advanced models in Southeast Asian data centers in order to access Nvidia chips unavailable in China. As these facilities become vital to Chinese AI developers’ ability to train advanced models, Beijing may come to view Chinese-operated data centers in ASEAN as strategic assets rather than ordinary overseas investments. As China’s Data Security Law authorizes countermeasures against countries that restrict Chinese investment or trade involving data technologies, any actions within those bounds by ASEAN governments could become a potential area of friction.
While there is no definitive proof that Beijing directs Chinese data centers abroad, the domestic intelligence and data security laws with which they must comply do complicate the idea that this infrastructure will always remain purely commercial. ASEAN’s focus on faster development and accessing its latent potential as a future digital economic power is understandable, especially when foreign providers offer capital, expertise, and capacity that domestic firms cannot yet match. But a digital economy built on systems governed elsewhere raises a basic question about how much digital sovereignty ASEAN actually retains. Affecting the norms upon which ASEAN’s nascent digital economies and AI ecosystems are built may pose a threat that member country governments may underestimate.
In short, ASEAN need not wholly reject the foreign capital and expertise driving its digital growth. Rather, ASEAN governments should diversify data center providers, clarify foreign data access obligations, focus on creating domestic AI capacity, and require full visibility into the flow of data into and out of the data center. They must also preserve the ability to audit operations and intervene if they uncover unauthorized access or foreign interference. Otherwise, member governments may retain the formal authority to write their own AI and privacy rules, but lose the practical ability to enforce them.

articles.title: Civil Society Groups File Lawsuit Against Indonesian Government Over Kalimantan Wildfires
articles.full_text:
The suit accuses President Prabowo Subianto and other senior officials of deliberate negligence for failing to prevent and properly handle the ongoing blazes.
The sun rises through wildfire haze in a town in Berau regency, in Indonesia’s East Kalimantan province, Aug. 20, 2026.
A group of ⁠indigenous ⁠and civil society organizations ⁠in Indonesia’s West Kalimantan province has filed a class-action ​lawsuit against the country’s government, accusing it of failing to prevent and handle the wildfires currently raging across the region.
The class action lawsuit was filed on September 17 at the Pontianak District Court by a coalition of civil groups known as Nafas Kalimantan Barat, which translates as “the breath of West Kalimantan,” Tempo reported.
The plaintiffs include the West Kalimantan chapter of the Indigenous Peoples Alliance of the Archipelago, the environmental group Laman Puyung Indonesia, and the leadership of the West Kalimantan Catholic Youth, as well as the citizen-activist Sisilius Rami.
The lawsuit names President Prabowo Subianto, Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the national police chief, and the head of the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB), as well as the governor and police chief of West Kalimantan, and the ministries of health, forestry, and environment.
It accuses them of deliberate negligence for failing to prevent and properly handle the ongoing wildfires, arguing that the disaster has overwhelmed provincial capacity. It also seeks a court order that would force the government to declare a national disaster, which would enable greater financial assistance for affected areas.
For months, Kalimantan has been battling its most intense wildfires since 2015. According to a report in The Guardian, “photos from Kalimantan have shown a thick, sepia-toned haze shrouding streets and obscuring cities, schoolchildren wearing masks at their desks, and even rescuers giving oxygen to smoke-affected orangutans.” Fires are also raging in Sumatra and in parts of Papua.
Since January, nearly 900,000 hectares have been burned across Indonesia, according to data from Nusantara Atlas, which tracks fires and deforestation in Asia. This falls short of the 2.6 million hectares that were destroyed in 2015, and the 1.65 million hectares that were consumed by wildfires in 2019, but Nusantara Atlas stated that burning usually accelerates in August and peaks during September and October, and that as of July 20, cumulative hotspot activity in 2026 “was above every previous year at the same point in the season.”
“Indonesia has not yet entered the period when fire activity has historically accelerated most sharply,” it stated. “The current hotspots signal is therefore an early warning, not yet the peak.” Indonesian Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni has warned that with a particularly extreme El Niño climate pattern only now starting to peak, September could be “when the real battle begins.”
Glorio Sanen, the lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the Jakarta Post that the spillover effects of peatland and forest fires in West Kalimantan – particularly the choking air pollution – continue to threaten public health and damage the environment.
“Meanwhile, our assessment concludes that there has been no sufficient coordination between the central government, ministries and even local administrations to prevent and respond to the disaster in West Kalimantan,” Glorio said.
The haze from the fires in Indonesia has now spread far beyond the country’s borders, including to the Malaysian states of Borneo, peninsular Malaysia, Brunei, Singapore, and the Philippines, affecting the health of millions. As of September 9, more than 113,000 people were reported to have suffered from wildfire-related respiratory illnesses.
Even if this year has been particularly bad for wildfires, the issue is an annual occurrence in Indonesia. As in other parts of Southeast Asia, the blazes are often deliberately lit in order to clear land for oil palm plantations and then spread raging infernos. Indonesia’s environment ministry says that it is investigating 19 companies that it believes may be linked to the wildfires, and has promised to punish any wrongdoers.
The fires have overwhelmed the Indonesian government’s capacity, in part due to the complexity of battling peatland fires. David Gaveau, a landscape ecologist who runs Nusantara Atlas, told The Guardian that fires on dried-out peatland are very difficult to extinguish, because they can burn for weeks underground. He described these fires as “the legacy of 50 years of forest degradation [and] deforestation” in Indonesia.
The initial hearing in the lawsuit is set for October 7.

articles.title: What Can Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman Gain From His Upcoming US Visit?
articles.full_text:
In Beijing, he met President Xi. Without a meeting with Trump or clear economic gains, the U.S. visit could fall short of Dhaka’s expectations.
Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman shakes hands with U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor during the latter’s visit to Bangladesh on Jul. 30-Aug. 1, 2026.
Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is traveling to the United States on September 21 to attend the U.N. General Assembly meeting.
Since February, when the Bangladesh Nationalist Party came to power, Rahman has visited Malaysia and China. This is his third international visit as prime minister.
Meanwhile, he didn’t join the BRICS summit in New Delhi. Officials said that Rahman was invited as BIMSTEC chair, not as prime minister of Bangladesh. As a result, he avoided the BRICS event.
U.S. President Donald Trump praised Rahman recently and thanked him for buying 25 Boeing aircraft. “Boeing will not let you down, and I will not forget,” Trump wrote in an August 31 letter to the prime minister. He also said he looked forward to meeting Rahman.
What is Rahman likely to achieve from his U.S. visit? Can he meet President Trump like he met Chinese President Xi Jinping? Officials are discussing a possible Trump meeting. The visit also gives Rahman a chance to seek U.S. investment and better trade terms following his talks in Beijing.
Bangladesh exported $7.74 billion in ready-made garments to the United States in FY 2025–26. This compares to the $1.3 billion of Bangladeshi goods that China imported across all categories in calendar year 2025. Although the figures cover different periods and product categories, they illustrate the importance of American buyers to Bangladesh.
Chinese loans and investment can help Bangladesh expand its industries and infrastructure, but China cannot replace the U.S. as a major export market. Beijing’s economic interests in Bangladesh also include Belt and Road Initiative projects and opportunities for Chinese companies.
Rahman has already outlined how China fits into his plans. At an investment forum in Beijing on June 25, he invited Chinese manufacturers to establish operations in Bangladesh and use the country to serve overseas markets. He also announced plans for an investment office in China. He pointed to Bangladesh’s suitability for production of goods for foreign buyers.
Rahman’s China visit also brought commitments on the Chinese economic zone in the port city of Chittagong, the modernization of Mongla port and work on the Teesta megaproject.
China and Bangladesh also agreed to hold strategic talks and explore a “2+2” dialogue, bringing together foreign and defense ministry officials. They also agreed to expand military exchanges, visits, and training.
Rahman is trying to deepen economic ties with both Washington and Beijing. The challenge is that some of the terms attached to closer cooperation with one could limit how far Bangladesh can go with the other.
The reciprocal trade agreement signed on February 9 gives Rahman a problem to address. Signed by the interim government just three days before the general election that brought Rahman’s BNP to power, it drew objections over both its terms and its timing. In April, independent parliamentarian Rumeen Farhana demanded parliamentary scrutiny, arguing that the decision should have waited for an elected government.
The February agreement reduced the U.S. reciprocal tariff on Bangladeshi goods from 20 to 19 percent. It also created a mechanism under which a specified volume of Bangladeshi garments made using U.S. cotton or man-made fiber could be exempted from the reciprocal tariff, although regular import duties could still apply.
In return, Bangladesh committed to facilitating about $15 billion in U.S. energy purchases over 15 years and an estimated $3.5 billion in agricultural purchases. The agricultural commitments include at least 700,000 tons of wheat annually for five years, at least $1.25 billion or 2.6 million tons of soy and soy products over one year, as well as purchases of U.S. cotton.
The February agreement could also complicate Bangladesh’s ties with China. It says that Washington could end the trade deal if Bangladesh signed an agreement giving special trade benefits to a “non-market country,” a term understood to include China. This does not ban Chinese investment in Bangladesh. But it could leave Rahman facing a difficult choice: pursue a trade agreement with Beijing and risk losing the benefits offered by the U.S.
Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir said in March that problematic provisions could be amended through further negotiation. Rahman could raise these concerns during his U.S. visit: clarify exporters’ benefits, seek flexibility over purchase commitments and establish what the China-related conditions would mean in practice. Renegotiation has not been confirmed as an item on the agenda of Rahman’s visit, but securing agreement to review these questions would give him something substantive to take home.
There is also an investment agenda for Rahman to pursue. During his July 30-August 1 visit to Bangladesh, U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor discussed expanding investment through the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation. He also told Rahman that American investors were interested in organizing a U.S. investor summit in Bangladesh and that he was working to facilitate it.
Gor separately offered to help resume U.S. Food and Drug Administration testing activities in Bangladesh. This is more directly a trade and market-access issue than an investment initiative, particularly for pharmaceutical and other FDA-regulated exports seeking access to the U.S. market.
The investment discussions were followed by a visit from a large U.S.-Bangladesh Business Council delegation in August. AmCham Bangladesh also told Rahman that it wanted to help mobilize another $5 billion in American investment over five years. Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir reiterated that target on September 12, saying the government and AmCham would work together to attract the investment.
Gor also proposed Bangladesh’s future participation in Pax Silica, the U.S.-led initiative covering artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and critical mineral supply chains. That gives Rahman something specific to explore beyond garments and aircraft purchases.
Washington’s interest in Bangladesh’s cooperation with China is mainly with regard to defense. In February, the then-U.S. Ambassador to Dhaka Brent Christensen told Reuters that the U.S. intended to offer Bangladesh American and allied military systems as alternatives to Chinese equipment.
However, by June, Dhaka and Beijing had agreed to explore a dialogue bringing together their foreign and defense establishments. Rahman therefore approaches American security discussions with an expanding Chinese relationship already underway.
Bangladeshi leaders have long used U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) visits to engage Washington. In 1974, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman met U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger in New York before traveling to Washington for talks with President Gerald Ford, helping build relations with the U.S. that had soured substantially during the 1971 Liberation War. Former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia also met Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice during her 2005 UNGA visit, although available reporting does not establish a major economic agreement resulting from that meeting.
Former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s experience showed both the opportunities and limits of these encounters. In 2017, she briefly raised the Rohingya crisis with Trump but afterwards said she didn’t expect help from him on the refugee issue, citing his administration’s restrictive stance on accepting refugees. Washington announced nearly $32 million in additional humanitarian assistance that week, though it cannot be attributed directly to their conversation.
More recently, Muhammad Yunus, who attended the UNGA meeting as chief adviser of the interim administration in September 2024, secured explicit U.S. support for his government during the bilateral meeting with President Biden. His immediate gain was political backing during a difficult transition.
Rahman has already met Xi in Beijing. A meeting with Trump would give him another achievement on the foreign front that he can point to at home. It could also help him build support for Bangladesh’s trade and investment goals in both countries. A UNGA visit, however, offers no guarantee of presidential access. Progress on the February trade agreement, particularly its implications for cooperation with China, or firm investment commitments could still make the trip worthwhile.
Without a meeting with Trump or clear economic gains, Rahman’s U.S. visit could end up being less successful than his trip to Beijing.
Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is traveling to the United States on September 21 to attend the U.N. General Assembly meeting.
articles.summary: In Beijing, he met President Xi. Without a meeting with Trump or clear economic gains, the U.S. visit could fall short of Dhaka's expectations.

articles.title: Malaysian King Approves Imprisoned Former PM Najib’s House Arrest Bid
articles.full_text:
The royal pardon is likely to empower the United Malays National Organization (UMNO) and widen the rifts within Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s reformist coalition.
On Friday, Malaysia’s king granted imprisoned former Prime Minister Najib Razak a royal pardon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his prison term under house arrest, prompting an outcry and creating another potential political headache for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.
Najib, 73, has been imprisoned since August 2022, when Malaysia’s top court upheld a conviction in a case linked to the multi-billion-dollar looting of the state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
In a statement, the government confirmed that Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar had granted Najib a “conditional pardon.” This will allow him to serve the remainder of his prison term under house arrest if he pays a 50 million ringgit fine ($12 million) imposed by the courts. Najib’s sentence expires on August 23, 2028.
The 1MDB state investment fund was established shortly after Najib’s election in 2009. In the ensuing years, Malaysian investigators claim, at least $4.5 billion was drained from the fund and laundered by Najib’s associates through a labyrinth of dummy corporations and bank accounts across the globe. The 1MDB scandal helped bring down Najib’s government at the general election of 2018, and has since led to criminal investigations in a number of other countries, including the United States, Switzerland, and Singapore.
Najib’s original conviction was handed down in 2020, when a court sentenced him to 12 years in prison and fined him 210 million ringgit ($51.5 million) for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust, and money laundering. The charges related to Najib’s illegal receipt of around $10 million from SRC International, a former unit of 1MDB.
Since then, Najib has pursued a range of legal and political tactics in order to reduce his sentence. In early 2024, he succeeded in gaining a royal pardon from Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah of Pahang, the country’s previous king, which halved his prison sentence and reduced his fine to 50 million ringgit. He has also mounted a legal bid to serve his sentence under house arrest, claiming that the royal pardon contained a royal “addendum order” that entitled him to serve the remainder of his sentence at ​home. Accusing the authorities of deliberately ignoring or concealing the order, he initiated legal action aiming to compel them to confirm its existence and to execute it. His legal bid was shot down by the Kuala Lumpur High Court in December 2025.
This royal pardon, based on the sweeping powers granted to the king under Malaysia’s constitution, effectively overrides that decision. As the Associated Press noted, the king’s decision “marked an unprecedented use of house arrest as a form of royal clemency in Malaysia and could renew debate over the rule of law and the treatment of Malaysia’s most prominent corruption convict.”
Indeed, much Malaysian social media commentary about the decision has been shot through with a resigned and weary acceptance that the rich and powerful will always manage to evade accountability.
G25, a prominent civil society coalition, said in a statement that it was “deeply shocked and dismayed” by the decision.
“This does nothing to strengthen public confidence in our criminal justice system. It is a travesty of justice,” the group said, adding that it was difficult to reconcile with the government’s stated commitment to strengthening the rule of law and combating corruption.”
Indeed, the decision has placed Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in a tricky position. While he has spent much of his career crusading against corruption, he is currently governing in a marriage-of-convenience coalition with Najib’s party, the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), the primary component of the Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition.
Given the various corruption scandals that have swirled around UMNO and its key figures, this has been a source of growing discontent within Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) and among its supporters, who argue that the Malaysian leader has been forced to compromise his principles in order to mollify his coalition partner.
This has reached a tipping point over the past year due to a string of corruption scandals, including the dismissal in January of 47 corruption charges against UMNO head Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, a key Anwar ally, and subsequent reports of widespread misconduct at the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission. This disillusionment arguably contributed to PH’s defeat in a string of important state-level elections over the past year.
In the wake of Najib’s pardon, Transport Minister Anthony Loke announced that he would tender his resignation, stating that the king’s decision, while legitimate, was “difficult to accept” for his Democratic Action Party (DAP), an important member of the PH coalition. The DAP, a party associated with Malaysia’s ethnic Chinese population, has performed poorly in the recent state elections due in part to the growing disillusionment with Anwar’s administration. In the wake of the recent state election results, some within the party have called for it to withdraw from the unity government in order to maintain its credibility as a liberal and reformist party. Last month, the DAP called a special congress to vote on the question. While the party’s members chose to stick with Anwar for now, it remains to be seen whether it will do so over the longer term.
At the same time, Najib’s release into house arrest would be a boon for UMNO and BN, which, while remaining in coalition with PH at the federal level, have competed with it in the recent state elections. In Negeri Sembilan, UMNO cooperated closely with the Islamist party PAS, a key member of the opposition Perikatan Nasional coalition, on a joint Malay unity platform, and won a significant majority in the state assembly. This offered a possible preview of the next general election, which is due by February 2028 – unless the growing PH-BN tensions prompt Anwar to call an earlier snap election.
On Friday, Anwar urged the public to accept the king’s decision, which he said would not weaken the government’s fight against graft and abuse of power.
“I want to stress that the principle of the rule of law remains intact,” he said, according to the AP. “Our commitment to taking action against all cases of corruption is not affected, and this does not mean the country should bow to practices of embezzlement and corruption.”
It remains unclear for now whether Najib will be able to fulfill the conditions necessary to secure his release from prison. A statement issued by Najib’s legal team yesterday said that the former leader was “profoundly grateful” to those who had offered their support and assistance. However, the question of whether he will be able to pay the required fine “does not lie in his own hands” given that many of his assets have been frozen due to the ongoing court cases.
“In those circumstances, our client is presently taking advice and considering his options as to how best to give effect to the condition,” the statement added.
After the royal clemency was announced, UMNO launched a “solidarity fund” in order to help, which had raised more than 1 million ringgit as of Saturday.
In the statement, Najib’s lawyers said that their client “does not wish the party, its members and supporters, or members of the public to feel burdened or obliged on his account.” He nonetheless remained “profoundly grateful” to all those who had “chosen to offer their support and assistance.”
As things stand, a lot of uncertainties surround Najib’s house arrest situation. Legal experts say that Malaysia does not have rules governing house arrest, and even if these are hastily put in place, it remains unclear how any potential breaches would be monitored or enforced.
However, there is a broad consensus that the pardon is unlikely to apply to the separate 15-year prison sentence handed down to Najib in a larger 1MDB-related trial late last year. In this case, judges found Najib guilty of 25 charges, including four counts of abuse of power and 21 counts of money laundering relating to 1MDB funds worth 2.27 billion ringgit ($574 million). Najib was also hit with a massive fine of 11.38 billion ringgit ($2.9 billion).
That prison term is due to begin after he completes his current sentence. Najib has appealed the verdict.

articles.title: India’s New Eye in the Sky: EOS-05 Satellite and What It Means for South Asia
articles.full_text:
EOS-05 is a single satellite that is part of a broader imitative of India to strengthen its ISR capabilities.
The Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) recently launched a new surveillance satellite designated as EOS-05 into geosynchronous earth orbit (GEO). The launch was carried out with the GSLV-F17 rocket.
The satellite – launched on September 4 – is the first earth observation satellite deployed in GEO by India. The satellite will allow New Delhi to continuously observe the subcontinent from an altitude ranging between 34,903 km and 35,884 km. The chairman of ISRO, V. Narayanan, said that “EOS-05 will become India’s first dedicated imaging satellite from the geo orbit providing important strategic data for the country.” 
The launch of the satellite is part of India’s long-term plan to strengthen its intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capabilities. The satellite will provide India with the capability to persistently track military movements in the subcontinent – especially Pakistan’s naval warships, aircraft, strategic assets movements, and force mobilization during crisis time. A new eye in the sky is an important military asset for India and can increase its counterforce capabilities in the age of emerging and disruptive technologies. 
India’s current space architecture consists of navigation, communication, ISR, and scientific satellites. For the purpose of communication, India has three dedicated military satellites – two of which are used by the Indian Navy and one by the Indian Air Force. Besides this, India has around 10 satellites that are dual-capable and can be used for military communication. The Indian navigation satellitessystem – known as Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) – has three operational satellites, IRNSS-1B, IRNSS-1I , and NVS-01. However, for basic positioning service four satellites are required in orbit ; the next satellite NVS-03 would be launched soon. The Indian ISR architecture consists of the CROSAT series for Optical purposes, the RISAT and NISAR series for SAR purposes, and the EMISAT satellite for Electronic ISR. The newly launched EOS-05 would be India’s first ISR satellite that would give real-time persistent observation of the subcontinent. 
In 2024, India’s Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) approved the Space Based Surveillance Phase-III (SBS-III) program that aimed to deploy 52 defense satellites into low-earth orbit (LEO) and geostationary orbit for surveillance. Under this project, ISRO will deploy 21 satellites and the private sector will develop 31 satellites. 
After the May 2025 crisis, there have been calls within the Indian strategic community to further strengthen Indian military capabilities in the space domain. For example, former Indian Chief of Defense Staff General Anil Chauhan, speaking at the Indian Defense Space Symposium (IDS) 2026, stressed the importance of military space based assets. He said, “If we fail in space, we will be forced to fight blind. However, if we dominate in space, we will fight with foresight.” 
The statement reflects a transformation in India’s strategic thinking vis-à-vis the military utility of space. The evolving character of warfare necessitates strengthening ISR architecture for maintaining persistent surveillance of strategically important areas both during peacetime and crisis situations. 
The newly launched EOS-05 satellite is particularly important as it adds to the persistent surveillance layer of India’s existing ISR architecture. Currently, India’s satellites are mainly in LEO, where they provide high-resolution imagery but have limitations because of rapid movement across the earth’s surface. EOS-05 being in geosynchronous orbit will provide prolonged observation of the subcontinent. This capability will strengthen India’s precision-strike capacity, as precision-strike missiles not only depend on range and accuracy but also timely information regarding the location of targets. Thus, in the broader sensor-to-shooter chain of network-centric warfare, space-based surveillance would play an important role. 
Moreover, persistent eyes in the sky can also strengthen India’s counterforce capabilities for both conventional and strategic purposes. For Pakistan, the implications of India strengthening ISR architecture and enhanced counterforce capabilities are direct. A persistent Indian eye in the sky would give its tri-services a near real-time picture of Pakistani naval deployments in the Arabian Sea, aircraft movements, and the dispersal of mobile missile launchers. As the survivability of mobile systems rests largely on their concealment, continuous wide-area surveillance, combined with high-resolution follow-up, shortens the time between detecting a target and striking it. India’s growing arsenal of long-range precision-strike missiles may become far more threatening with an added eye in space. 
Moreover, there are also benefits to India of the new satellite system for defensive purposes. It can also help India be better prepared for a counterstrike by Pakistan, especially with an advanced missile defense system. Having persistent capability to monitor movements of Pakistan’s troops, India can be more prepared to defend itself. 
However, this can have implications for South Asian deterrence dynamics. Faster detection, enhanced targeting information, and better precision-strike capabilities would lead to a compression of decision-making timelines during crisis. Because of territorial contiguity between India and Pakistan, decision-making timelines are already very short. Thus, increasing vulnerability of strategic assets to detection can induce Pakistan to early dispersal, mobilization, and further concealment of its military assets. This can also create a “use-it-or-lose-it dilemma” and further increases the risks of miscalculation and inadvertent escalation. Thus, enhanced space-based ISR capabilities can help in increasing situational awareness but would present new challenges for crisis stability and escalation management in South Asia.
In conclusion, EOS-05 is a single satellite that is part of a broader imitative of India to strengthen its ISR capabilities under the SBS-III program. However, its launching points toward an Indian strategic shift from periodic snapshots to persistent watch, and this enhancement of capability can have implications on how the next crisis between India and Pakistan will unfold. Islamabad has to further strengthen survivability of its conventional and strategic assets through concealment, deception, and mobility practices.

Besides this, India has around 10 satellites that are dual-capable and can be used for military communication. The Indian navigation satellitessystem – known as Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) – has three operational satellites, IRNSS-1B, IRNSS-1I , and NVS-01. However, for basic positioning service four satellites are required in orbit ; the next satellite NVS-03 would be launched soon. The Indian ISR architecture consists of the CROSAT series for Optical purposes, the RISAT and NISAR series for SAR purposes, and the EMISAT satellite for Electronic ISR. The newly launched EOS-05 would be India’s first ISR satellite that would give real-time persistent observation of the subcontinent. 
In 2024, India’s Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) approved the Space Based Surveillance Phase-III (SBS-III) program that aimed to deploy 52 defense satellites into low-earth orbit (LEO) and geostationary orbit for surveillance. Under this project, ISRO will deploy 21 satellites and the private sector will develop 31 satellites. 
After the May 2025 crisis, there have been calls within the Indian strategic community to further strengthen Indian military capabilities in the space domain. For example, former Indian Chief of Defense Staff General Anil Chauhan, speaking at the Indian Defense Space Symposium (IDS) 2026, stressed the importance of military space based assets. He said, “If we fail in space, we will be forced to fight blind. However, if we dominate in space, we will fight with foresight.” 
The statement reflects a transformation in India’s strategic thinking vis-à-vis the military utility of space. The evolving character of warfare necessitates strengthening ISR architecture for maintaining persistent surveillance of strategically important areas both during peacetime and crisis situations. 
The newly launched EOS-05 satellite is particularly important as it adds to the persistent surveillance layer of India’s existing ISR architecture. Currently, India’s satellites are mainly in LEO, where they provide high-resolution imagery but have limitations because of rapid movement across the earth’s surface. EOS-05 being in geosynchronous orbit will provide prolonged observation of the subcontinent. This capability will strengthen India’s precision-strike capacity, as precision-strike missiles not only depend on range and accuracy but also timely information regarding the location of targets. Thus, in the broader sensor-to-shooter chain of network-centric warfare, space-based surveillance would play an important role. 
Moreover, persistent eyes in the sky can also strengthen India’s counterforce capabilities for both conventional and strategic purposes. For Pakistan, the implications of India strengthening ISR architecture and enhanced counterforce capabilities are direct. A persistent Indian eye in the sky would give its tri-services a near real-time picture of Pakistani naval deployments in the Arabian Sea, aircraft movements, and the dispersal of mobile missile launchers. As the survivability of mobile systems rests largely on their concealment, continuous wide-area surveillance, combined with high-resolution follow-up, shortens the time between detecting a target and striking it. India’s growing arsenal of long-range precision-strike missiles may become far more threatening with an added eye in space. 
Moreover, there are also benefits to India of the new satellite system for defensive purposes. It can also help India be better prepared for a counterstrike by Pakistan, especially with an advanced missile defense system. Having persistent capability to monitor movements of Pakistan’s troops, India can be more prepared to defend itself. 
However, this can have implications for South Asian deterrence dynamics. Faster detection, enhanced targeting information, and better precision-strike capabilities would lead to a compression of decision-making timelines during crisis. Because of territorial contiguity between India and Pakistan, decision-making timelines are already very short. Thus, increasing vulnerability of strategic assets to detection can induce Pakistan to early dispersal, mobilization, and further concealment of its military assets. This can also create a “use-it-or-lose-it dilemma” and further increases the risks of miscalculation and inadvertent escalation. Thus, enhanced space-based ISR capabilities can help in increasing situational awareness but would present new challenges for crisis stability and escalation management in South Asia.
In conclusion, EOS-05 is a single satellite that is part of a broader imitative of India to strengthen its ISR capabilities under the SBS-III program. However, its launching points toward an Indian strategic shift from periodic snapshots to persistent watch, and this enhancement of capability can have implications on how the next crisis between India and Pakistan will unfold. Islamabad has to further strengthen survivability of its conventional and strategic assets through concealment, deception, and mobility practices. 
The Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) recently launched a new surveillance satellite designated as EOS-05 into geosynchronous earth orbit (GEO). The launch was carried out with the GSLV-F17 rocket.
The satellite – launched on September 4 – is the first earth observation satellite deployed in GEO by India. The satellite will allow New Delhi to continuously observe the subcontinent from an altitude ranging between 34,903 km and 35,884 km. The chairman of ISRO, V. Narayanan, said that “EOS-05 will become India’s first dedicated imaging satellite from the geo orbit providing important strategic data for the country.” 
Abdul Moiz Khan works as a research officer at Center for International Strategic Studies, Islamabad.
Sher Ali Kakar serves as an associate director at the Balochistan Think Tank Network (BTTN), at BUITEMS, Quetta.
articles.summary: EOS-05 is a single satellite that is part of a broader imitative of India to strengthen its ISR capabilities.

articles.title: Abroad, India’s RSS Speaks of ‘Love.’ At Home, Its Affiliates Attack Christians.
articles.full_text:
From church vandalism to grave desecration, assaults against Christian minorities are increasing in the large state of West Bengal since the BJP, an RSS offshoot, came to power in May.
Screenshot of a Facebook livestream shows the altercation at Goutam Bera’s residence in Ranichak village, West Bengal, Aug. 26, 2026.
Sutahata is a rural place in the eastern Indian state of West Bengal, which has been ruled by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) since the May 2026 state elections. There, on August 26, about 50 people gathered at Goutam Bera’s residence in Ranichak village. It was a house fellowship gathering that involved Bible study and prayer. Many attendees were Hindus, mostly friends and acquaintances of the Bera family.
The news of the gathering reached members of Hindu supremacist organizations. One of them broadcast a live video on Facebook while on his way to Bera’s place. They had heard a Christian priest had gone there to convert Hindus. “Let’s see what they are up to,” he said. By the time the livestreamer reached Bera’s house, some of his fellows were already there. They barged into the house, abused those present and threw people out, before allegedly manhandling the rest of the attendees.
“You are Hindus. You have idols of Hindu deities at home. How could you bring in a Father and practice Christianity?” one can be heard shouting. “They have started this Jesus business now. See, we have recovered a Bible! My God, they have a Bible here!” 
One video shows the intruders – carrying saffron flags – ordering the prayer attendees, rather rudely and loudly, to chant “Hare Krishna, Hare Ram” and “Jai Shree Ram.” Another video shows the cops taking the prayer attendees to a police vehicle. At one point, people from the crowd can be heard shouting: “Thrash them, thrash them!” 
According to Joy Kumar Ghughu, the pastor who was reading from the Bible, the police first took 17 prayer attendees, including him, to the Sutahata block primary health center for treatment and a medical check-up. They were then taken to the Sutahata police station, where everyone was interrogated about the intention behind the gathering. Their mobile phones were examined. At about 8 p.m., they were told they could go. 
“We did not lodge any police complaint against the attackers because Jesus teaches forgiveness. We will pray for their well-being,” Ghughu told The Diplomat. 
He, however, asked why propagating Christianity should be objected to, when Article 25 of the Indian Constitution says that all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practice and propagate their religion freely. “We are not paying anyone to become Christians,” Ghughu said. 
Senior BJP leader Amit Malviya described the incident, along with two others, as “isolated local objections to prayer gatherings… peacefully resolved by the police.” However, videos posted on social media platforms by those involved in the attack tell a different story.  
The intruders identified themselves as members of Shree Ram Janmotsab Samity (Lord Ram birthday celebration committee). The Samity does not hide its links to the RSS, the BJP’s ideological and organizational parent. Its Facebook page regularly posts invites to events of the RSS and its affiliates, like the Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP). 
At Sutahata, a person recording on the spot identified himself and his fellows as belonging to the VHP. Showing videos of the organizers of the prayer gathering and the pastor present there, one of them told the video’s audience: “Beat them up with brooms whenever and wherever you see them. They are worse than terrorists.” 
In another video from the incident, uploaded to a Facebook page of Bajrang Dal, the youth wing of the VHP, the intruders said: “We are from VHP Chaitanyapur unit… Sanatan Dharma is the world’s greatest religion. Whenever you spot people we identified in our videos, just inform us.” The Hindu supremacists usually refer to Hinduism as Sanatan Dharma (eternal religion). 
A few hours later, in a Facebook post, the Samity said, “Let this serve as a warning to those who spread religious propaganda under the guise of ‘God the Father’: if we catch you, you will face severe consequences.”
Its based on actions like these that a recent database described the RSS family of organizations, popularly called the Sangh Parivar, as “the largest far-right network in history.” 
Modi called the RSS the world’s largest NGO (non-governmental organization).
That discrepancy gets to the heart of the RSS’s attempt to paint a very different picture of itself abroad.
Hindu civilizational identity rests on the idea that diversity and unity can coexist, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat said in London at the beginning of September. “We must never lose sight of the fact that we are one.”
During a September 6 event in London as part of a U.S.-Canada-U.K. tour marking the organization’s centenary, Bhagwat said, “I heard some people say intense hatred is the basis of our work. It is just the reverse. ‘Shuddha Satvik Prem’ (pure and divine love) is the basis of our work.” 
Before landing in London, he had visited New York and Toronto. In New York, while addressing  a “Universal Oneness Celebration” at Madison Square Garden on August 29, Bhagwat said, “To call oneself Hindu, one must believe that all paths lead to the same destination and that every human has dignity, with no difference between human beings.” He described diversity as a “decoration for our innate unity” that has to be accepted: “It has to be respected. It has to be protected.”
In West Bengal, the next day, activists belonging to different RSS-linked organizations disrupted three separate Christian prayer gatherings and abused and heckled the prayer participants.
Here are some of the incidents, in just one Indian state, that took place during the same weeks Bhagwat was spreading the message of love and oneness abroad: 
August 23: A mob broke into a church premises at Uluberia in Howrah district, vandalized the prayer room, and attacked several prayer attendees. Bajrang Dal activists went to close down a Christian house prayer ceremony at Baniberia area in Mograhat of South 24 Parganas district. 
August 30: Bajrang Dal activists thrashed a lawyer for hosting Christian prayers at his residence in Baripur, South 24-Parganas. Miscreants stormed the Sunday prayer gathering at Jagatballabhpur, Howrah district. Another prayer venue was vandalized at Hingalganj in North 24 Parganas.  
September 1: Hindu Jagran Manch, another RSS affiliate, locked up a school run by Christians at Hasnabad Rupomari bazar in North 24 Parganas district. Protesters told the media: “Their walls are full of Jesus’ photos! No Hindu deities at all! Why should it be so? Why are they teaching kids about Jesus’ life? This school must be closed down.”
September 7: A group of activists claiming to be from the VHP and BD interrupted a prayer gathering at a tiny, makeshift church in Bally of Howrah district and told them that preaching Christianity will not be allowed. 
September 9: People identifying themselves as VHP and BD organizers reached a house at Mograhat area in South 24-Parganas district, aggressively quizzed people about who they worship, and objected to praying before Jesus. 
September 11: Bajrang Dal activists threatened the organizers of another prayer gathering at Mamudpur in Mograhat, South 24 Parganas. 
September 12: VHP activists threatened members of a house prayer gathering at Taldi, Canning, South 24 Parganas, ordered them to tear all of Jesus’ photos apart and sternly told them to stop the gathering for good. “Why Jesus? Why Jesus? Why Jesus?” they kept shouting. “Whoever you may be going to complain to, tell them that we are from VHP and Bajrang Dal. We’ll see who holds how much power.”  
The next day, another video went viral on social media that showed a Hindu supremacist mob violently abusing prayer gatherers and publicly tearing apart books on Param-pita (God the Father). “What the hell is ‘God the Father’? Why don’t you read the Gita or chant Hare Krishna?” the attackers shouted as they tore apart books on Christian faith.
articles.summary: From church vandalism to grave desecration, assaults against Christian minorities are increasing in the large state of West Bengal since the BJP, an RSS offshoot, came to power in May.

articles.title: From Symbolism to Strategy: The Expanding Operational Role of Women in Baloch Militancy
articles.full_text:
The motivations of individual women who join militant organizations cannot be reduced to a single explanation. The organizational incentives are easier to identify.
On May 22, the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), one of the principal armed groups in Pakistan’s Baloch insurgency, announced the formation of a dedicated women’s wing and named Shaynaz Baloch as its commander. The announcement was significant not simply because it placed a woman in a more visible position within the organization, but because it appeared to formalize a trend that has been developing since 2022: the expansion of women’s participation in Baloch militancy from largely symbolic and support roles into direct operational activity.
The development raises a broader question: Why are Baloch militant organizations expanding women’s roles now, and what does this mean for an insurgency historically dominated by men?
The shift can be traced most clearly to April 2022, when Shari Baloch carried out a suicide attack at the Confucius Institute at the University of Karachi, killing three Chinese teachers and their Pakistani driver. The BLA claimed responsibility and presented her as its first female suicide operative. Since then, several other women have been linked to suicide operations attributed to BLA factions. In June 2023, Sumaiya Qalandrani Baloch carried out a suicide attack targeting a military convoy in Turbat. In August 2024, a woman identified by the BLA as Mahal Baloch conducted a vehicle-borne attack against a Frontier Corps facility in Bela. In March 2025, Mahikhan Baloch carried out another suicide attack against a paramilitary convoy in Kalat.  
In November 2025, the trend extended to another major Baloch armed group, the Baloch Liberation Front (BLF), when Zareena Rafiq carried out a vehicle-borne attack against a Frontier Corps facility in Nokundi. The pattern suggests that the use of women is no longer confined to an isolated form of militant propaganda. It is becoming part of how some Baloch armed groups recruit, operate, and present themselves. 
The development became even more visible during the BLA’s January-February 2026 offensive, which the organization called Operation Herof 2.0. The BLA publicized the participation of several women in the coordinated attacks, including female suicide operatives.
Balochistan, Pakistan’s largest province by area and one of its least densely populated, has experienced successive waves of Baloch nationalist insurgency, with the current conflict emerging in the early 2000s. The BLA and BLF are among the principal separatist organizations involved. They frame their campaigns around grievances including political marginalization, resource distribution, and alleged abuses by the Pakistani state. Pakistani authorities classify the groups as terrorist organizations and have attributed aspects of the insurgency to external support. The conflict has also acquired a significant international dimension. Balochistan hosts Gwadar Port and other major infrastructure associated with the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), making Chinese nationals and projects recurring targets for Baloch militants.
For much of the current insurgency, however, women associated with Baloch nationalism were more visible in political activism, advocacy, and community mobilization than in armed operations. Organizations such as the Baloch Students Organization-Azad (BSO-A) and the Baloch Yakjehti Committee have provided platforms for campaigns concerning enforced disappearances, alleged extrajudicial killings, and other grievances involving the Pakistani state. Women such as Mahrang Baloch and Sammi Deen Baloch have subsequently become prominent advocates on these issues. Karima Mehrab Baloch, who became the first woman to chair BSO-A, was another prominent figure in Baloch nationalist activism before she died in Toronto in December 2020.
This established a largely political role for women within the broader Baloch nationalist movement. But the emergence of women in militant operations since 2022 marks a departure from that pattern. The May announcement of a dedicated women’s wing in the BLA represents a potential further step in this evolution, from individual female participation in militant operations toward a more formal organizational role. 
The motivations of individual women who join militant organizations cannot be reduced to a single explanation. Political grievances, personal experiences, family or social networks, ideological commitment, trauma, and the search for purpose can all influence recruitment. These factors differ from one individual to another.
The organizational incentives are easier to identify. Women can provide militant groups with additional operational flexibility. Gendered assumptions about who constitutes a security threat can affect how individuals are screened, monitored, or approached by security personnel. This does not make women inherently better operatives. Rather, it gives organizations another category of personnel through which they can attempt to exploit gaps in security practices. Female participation can also broaden the pool from which militant organizations recruit. It allows groups to portray their struggle as extending beyond young male fighters and into families and communities.
The propaganda value may be even more important. A female militant challenges the conventional image of an insurgent as a young man carrying a weapon. Baloch militant groups have used photographs, videos, and biographies of female operatives to portray their participation as evidence that the conflict has reached across gender and social boundaries.
However, reducing female militants to passive victims of manipulation obscures their agency and the possibility that some make deliberate ideological or political choices. At the same time, focusing exclusively on agency can obscure the organizational structures that recruit, train, indoctrinate, and deploy them. The analytical challenge is to account for both. 
The Baloch case is part of a much broader history of women’s participation in political violence. Research on female suicide bombers has documented substantial participation by women in conflicts ranging from the Middle East to South Asia and Southeast Asia. Secular separatist organizations such as the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) were among the groups that developed significant roles for women in their military structures. The LTTE incorporated women into combat units and became particularly associated with female suicide operations. The PKK likewise developed extensive female military and organizational structures. 
Later, jihadist organizations including Boko Haram, al-Shabaab, and the Islamic State expanded women’s roles in different ways, including recruitment, propaganda, logistics, and, in some cases, direct participation in attacks. The comparison should not be overstated, however. These organizations differ substantially in ideology, structure, social environment, and strategic objectives. Baloch armed groups are primarily ethno-nationalist and separatist organizations rather than transnational jihadist movements. 
The expansion of women’s participation comes amid a broader deterioration in Pakistan’s security environment. The Baloch insurgency is only one component of that deterioration; the resurgence of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), particularly along the Afghan border, has also contributed substantially to the country’s terrorism burden.
The Global Terrorism Index 2026 ranked Pakistan as the country most affected by terrorism in 2025, recording 1,139 terrorism-related deaths and 1,045 incidents. Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa together accounted for more than 74 percent of terrorist attacks and 67 percent of terrorism-related deaths recorded in Pakistan that year. This wider context matters because the emergence of female militants could tempt security institutions toward an overly broad response.
The answer is not simply increased surveillance of women. A poorly designed response could stigmatize women participating in legitimate political activity and further blur the distinction between peaceful activism and militancy. Instead, intelligence assessments should account for women as potential participants across the spectrum of militant activity, including recruitment, propaganda, financing, logistics, and direct operations. At the same time, investigators must distinguish genuine indicators of militant involvement from political dissent, human rights activism, and ordinary civic activity.
That distinction is particularly important in Balochistan, where a significant political and human rights movement exists alongside an armed insurgency. Conflating the two would not only threaten civil liberties; it could also make counterterrorism less effective by expanding the pool of people who feel alienated from the state. The strategic challenge is therefore twofold: prevent militant organizations from turning women’s visibility into an operational advantage, while ensuring that the state’s response does not itself deepen the alienation that those organizations seek to capitalize on. That means combining intelligence-led counterterrorism with community engagement, strategic communication, and efforts to address the grievances that militant organizations seek to exploit.
