articles.title: What’s Wrong With US Pacific Islands Policy?
articles.full_text:
The China-donated ship that is the only regular transport along the Yap island chain.
There is currently an active debate about U.S. policy in the Pacific Islands. Some are saying the U.S. is AWOL in the region. Others have said this is one of the most active times for U.S. engagement, including the Heritage Foundation, which just published a detailed “policy inventory” of announced U.S. activities in the region.
What do I think? Let me start in a Pacific Islands way, with a story.
In May 2025, I took a China-donated cargo ship from Yap to Woleai atoll, in the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM). Several hundred Micronesians (from babies to grandmothers), five Chinese construction workers, and I slept on the deck, used communal bathrooms, and ate the food we brought along for the days-long trip down the island chain. 
By the time I got back to Yap weeks later, I had lice, parasites, and a leg wound that took U.S. military-grade salve to heal. I also had friends for life. 
Why did I go? The U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) had announced around $2 billion in infrastructure investments on the main island of Yap State, an island also called Yap. Meanwhile, I had heard from Micronesian friends that the Chinese were working on something in Woleai, in a different part of Yap State.
There was also a Dolly Parton angle – but that’s for later. 
People in DoD assured me (and their superiors) that everything was fine. Knowing how the U.S. government operates in other parts of the Pacific, I wondered if they had the full picture. So, I packed a bag full of tins of Chef Boyardee, bottles of water, and Dramamine and went to take a look.
Soon after I arrived on Woleai, the president of FSM, Wesley Simina, arrived on his own boat. After the traditional beach greeting, he and his entourage disappeared on one of the island’s few pick-up trucks. His wife rode on the truck’s bed.
Local kids told me he had gone to the groundbreaking for the runway. The runway? I wanted to see, so they led me on a dash through a shortcut in the jungle, past overgrown machinery left behind from the years Woleai spent under the control of Imperial Japan.
Then the woods opened up, exposing the cracked runway first built by the Japanese, rows of Chinese heavy machinery, and a stage announcing the imminent groundbreaking.
While the president’s official schedule may have said he came to Woleai for the high school graduation, it wasn’t a coincidence that he was also on the island when a Chinese state-owned company began work to rebuild an Imperial Japanese runway just over 640 kilometers from Guam.
Based on reactions, key people in the U.S. government were caught by surprise. Their “Micronesia whisperers” had failed them.
A few days later, on a School of War podcast – an interview I conducted via Starlink, while I was a ten-minute walk from the Chinese workers’ barracks on Woleai – I commented the United States wasn’t listening to the right people, and there were going to be problems moving forward with the $2 billion investment in infrastructure in Yap, unless something changed.
On June 29, 2026, just over a year later, Admiral Samuel Paparo, the commander of U.S. Pacific Command (PACOM), wrote to FSM’s President Simina that, due to a breakdown in the negotiations, “U.S. PACOM intends to move forward by assessing alternative locations across the region to meet the needs of Pacific defense.”
That may just be a negotiation tactic. But the fact the situation has deteriorated to the point that a threat was deemed necessary is one indication that, in spite of the serious attempt by the Trump administration to work more – and better – with the Pacific Islands, it is not necessarily achieving the desired outcomes.
They should have asked Dolly Parton, the late country star and all-around American icon, for advice.
Dolly Parton, Habele, and More Untapped Wisdom
While on Woleai, I took an hour-long outboard motor boat trip to an island across the lagoon for an elementary school graduation. I had heard that Parton’s Imagination Library delivers free books to kids out there. It does, which was how I met Tasur.
Think about the social, political, bureaucratic and practical logistics involved in getting “The Little Engine That Could” from the U.S. state of Tennessee, where the Imagination Library is headquartered, into the hands of Tasur on Woleai. Someone helping Parton’s non-profit knows Yap well enough to do not just that, but to ensure hundreds of kids across Yap get a free book every month from Tennessee.
That “someone” is Neil Mellen and the team at Habele, an educational NGO that, for years, has provided not just free books, but scholarships and more to kids across FSM. Founded and funded by former Peace Corps volunteers and other Americans, its sister organization, Habele Research Institute, runs a comprehensive Wiki on Yap, which includes one of the largest online collections of historical material on the region.
If those involved in negotiating the U.S. military’s runway and port development didn’t read the Habele page on the topic  – and then ask to talk to the people who put it together – they might want to consider another line of work. I’m pretty sure they didn’t.
I do know they didn’t spend time talking to Father Francis X. Hezel – I asked him. Father Fran, as he’s called, now lives in Guam. He has been in region since the early 1960s and literally wrote the book(s) on Micronesia. U.S. policymakers used to go out of their way to meet with him regularly. 
Not anymore, even though PACOM’s Joint Task Force – Micronesia is also based in Guam.
Father Fran, an American Jesuit, set up Micronesia Seminar Library, a physical, comprehensive collection of books, video, articles, periodical, photos, and more covering the sweep of Micronesian history, culture, politics, etc. 
Father Rich McAuliff, another American Jesuit, has also been in Micronesia for years, and is on Yap taking care of the Library.
Given the changes to the local economy that $2 billion in investment might bring – Yap Island has a population of around 7,000 – it would also be helpful to talk to Americans in the business community, like Mark Hartman, about complexities around access to financing, human resources, logistics, land rights, the regulatory environment, etc. Hartman wrote a brief for Habele to try to inform the U.S.-Pacific Investment Summit. It is, as he says, the basics, but even that is usually overlooked. 
The DoD negotiators (and any others, including from the State Department, Interior Department, etc.) also would benefit from extensive conversations with the fine folks at Pacific Mission Aviation (PMA), a missionary airline that has been proving free medical evacuations, search and rescues, and more in Yap for over 50 years. 
PMA pilots, almost all American, are the only ones regularly using the Woleai airfield. They know every runway, rock, and reef in the region. Almost every family in Yap has a story about good done by the PMA. At the Ulithi high school graduation last year, Simina, the FSM president, was the opening act; it was Amos Collins, a PMA pilot, who gave the keynote.
As Brock Welge, the PMA’s director of maintenance, said in a recent interview: “Probably the biggest misconception people have is how long it takes to build relationships out here… I’ve been out here since 2019 and I’m just now starting to feel accepted and integrated into the community. Which is amazing – but it takes a long time to build those relationships, sometimes lifetimes.”
articles.summary: It’s the relationships, stupid.

articles.title: After a Self-Immolation at the UN, Rethinking What Beijing Fears on Tibet
articles.full_text:
Beijing’s real vulnerability is not international action. It’s rising awareness within the Chinese population.
Members of Chinese Youth Stand for Tibet attend a rally outside China’s consulate in San Francisco, the U.S., Aug. 20, 2026.
On July 2, Lobga Rangzen, a Tibetan man who had taken the word meaning “independence and freedom” as his name, set himself on fire outside the United Nations headquarters in New York. His act came one day after China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law took effect. In a video posted before his death, he denounced the law as an erasure of Tibetan identity and called on Tibetans-in-exile to take up their responsibility. 
He chose the spot deliberately, too. Tibetans have looked to the U.N. for redress since 1950, when Tibet’s appeal first went to the new global body. The General Assembly passed resolutions on Tibet in 1959, 1961, and 1965. The 1961 resolution explicitly invoked Tibetans’ right to self-determination. Yet after the People’s Republic took China’s U.N. seat in 1971, the issue vanished from the organization’s agenda. Rangzen’s self-immolation was an indictment of six decades of silence.
For weeks after his death, Tibetan communities across the globe marched and demonstrated. CNN, Radio Free Asia, and others covered it; the U.N. secretary-general’s spokesperson offered condolences, and the U.S. State Department reaffirmed its support for Tibetans. Then, within days, the coverage vanished. No government went beyond boilerplate statements of sympathy.
For decades, the Central Tibetan Administration’s envoys and Tibetan human rights organizations have worked in Geneva, Washington, and Brussels with extraordinary persistence, winning legislation like the Resolve Tibet Act. Beijing’s position has never varied: Tibet is an “inalienable part of China.” The one channel that did exist, nine rounds of talks with the Dalai Lama’s envoys between 2002 and 2010, produced nothing, and those talks have been moribund for over 15 years.
The strategy of seeking international support to enact change in Tibet has run its course. The world has heard Tibetans cry out since 1959. Sympathy has calcified into routine: statements, condemnations, calls for dialogue. There is little prospect that external pressure alone will move the Chinese Communist Party on Tibet, and no government has shown any willingness to go beyond words.
But Beijing fears a different kind of pressure, one that comes from inside the Chinese-speaking world.
A year ago, Chinese state security police in Changsha detained Zhang Yadi, a 22-year-old Han Chinese student who had been studying in France, on suspicion of “inciting separatism.” Her offense: writing and editing for Chinese Youth Stand for Tibet (华语青年挺藏会), a bilingual Han-Tibetan exchange platform I founded. Zhang was born and raised in Hunan, Mao’s home province, to Han parents. Nearly all of our members are also ethnically Han.
Many people asked why a Han Chinese person would risk prison for Tibetans. The more useful question is why Beijing treated a small volunteer media project as a state security threat and detained a college student over it. 
The CCP understands that its rule in Tibet rests not only on security spending but on the acquiescence of the Han majority – an acquiescence manufactured through decades of disinformation. Since 1959, state propaganda has taught Chinese citizens that old Tibet was a barbaric serf society, that the Dalai Lama was its greatest slaveholder. One particularly enduring myth holds that Tibet’s Buddhist monks made drums out of human skin. A hit 1990s song to that effect, “Sister Drum” (阿姐鼓), was written by a Han composer who knew the story only secondhand, from siblings who had traveled to Tibet. Chinese internet users still cite the song as evidence of Tibetan savagery. 
According to the CCP’s preferred narrative, the People’s Liberation Army was Tibet’s savior, and occupation is liberation. Ordinary Chinese people don’t defend the CCP’s Tibet policy out of malice; most sincerely see no case against it.
Han acceptance of this narrative is the foundation for CCP rule in Tibet – but it is more fragile than it looks. In 2025, the Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR) raised just 31.8 billion yuan in local revenue against 310 billion in spending. Central transfers of 253.88 billion yuan, more than 80 percent of the budget according to the TAR’s budget reports, filled the gap, funding both livelihood programs and a vast stability-maintenance apparatus. And that budget excludes spending in the Tibetan areas of Qinghai, Sichuan, Gansu, and Yunnan. 
There is already simmering resentment of these policies. On the Chinese internet, a segment of Han nationalists already ask why the government grants ethnic minorities college-entrance bonus points and what it derides as “super-citizen treatment.” As China’s economy slows, complaints about the fiscal burden are growing sharper. That resentment is combustible, as ready to turn on minorities as on the CCP. 
The party can ignore foreign condemnation, but not a public at home that calls into question Beijing’s rule in Tibet. Han Chinese who speak fluently to that public, using the Chinese language and Chinese platforms, are the CCP’s nightmare on the ethnic frontier. More and more Han Chinese resent CCP policies in Tibet. Our aim is to redirect the questions they are already asking. Instead of “why are we paying for them?” we ask: “What is this money actually buying, and who does it benefit?”
The Dalai Lama grasped the importance of Han Chinese partnerships decades ago. He appointed Chinese liaison officers at Tibetan offices worldwide and built his Middle Way Approach partly around winning Chinese hearts. But the CTA’s Chinese-language capacity has withered; the Chinese sections of exile institutions have become marginal afterthoughts. 
Our group, Chinese Youth for Tibet, formed organically on the Chinese-language internet, among young people fluent in its idiom. Tibetans welcomed us because that gap had gone unfilled for so long.
Other Han Chinese have taken up the cause before. Grace Wang, a Duke student, was buried in nationalist abuse in 2008 for merely trying to mediate between pro-Tibet and pro-China protesters. The late historian Li Jianglin, born into a Communist family, spent years recording exile Tibetans’ oral histories; her “Tibet in Agony” reconstructed why the Dalai Lama fled in 1959. In July, police in Lhasa detained Zhang Yi, a pro-democracy activist since 1989, for displaying a photograph of the Dalai Lama at Sera Monastery, and formally arrested him on July 28. 
One by one, Han Chinese keep arriving at a shared sense of historical responsibility. My moment came in 2018, while teaching at a Tibetan middle school; the government forcibly closed that school two years ago.
Yet groups like Chinese Youth for Tibet fall into an institutional blind spot. When Zhang Yadi was arrested, concern stopped at her as an individual; almost no Tibetan or Western outlet has interviewed our organization to ask what we do, or why Han Chinese would stand up for Tibet at all. Our proposals to foundations disappear without reply. A veteran colleague told me recently: you have fallen into the gap between two desks.
In international media, government bureaucracies, and foundations, the “Tibet desk” and the “China desk” are separate worlds. Most China specialists pay little attention to Tibet. Tibet specialists know little of Chinese administration, law, or society – especially in the Tibetan areas outside the TAR, where most Tibetans live. 
This gap explains why Chinese-speaking advocates for Tibet working to raise awareness using Chinese language platforms remain unfunded, uncovered, and unprotected – even as Beijing prosecutes our members as state security threats. The CCP takes our work seriously enough to prosecute it. Western foundations and newsrooms have yet to really register our existence. 
Han and Tibetan people have been neighbors for millennia. We drink from the same rivers, and our futures are bound together long after this regime is gone. For that reason, I believe the rise of Han Chinese-driven activism is one of the most strategically significant developments in the Tibet issue.
International advocacy kept Tibet’s cause alive for more than 70 years, and that work must continue. But the diminishing returns were made all too tragically obvious by Lobga Rangzen’s self-immolation. He burned to death on the U.N.’s front steps and the world barely noticed. 
The international community is not going to change Tibet’s fate. What could still make a difference is a growing awareness among China’s Chinese-speaking majority. Whoever wants to change Tibet’s future should start funding and covering the people doing this work, and protecting them.
On July 2, Lobga Rangzen, a Tibetan man who had taken the word meaning “independence and freedom” as his name, set himself on fire outside the United Nations headquarters in New York. His act came one day after China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law took effect. In a video posted before his death, he denounced the law as an erasure of Tibetan identity and called on Tibetans-in-exile to take up their responsibility. 
He chose the spot deliberately, too. Tibetans have looked to the U.N. for redress since 1950, when Tibet’s appeal first went to the new global body. The General Assembly passed resolutions on Tibet in 1959, 1961, and 1965. The 1961 resolution explicitly invoked Tibetans’ right to self-determination. Yet after the People’s Republic took China’s U.N. seat in 1971, the issue vanished from the organization’s agenda. Rangzen’s self-immolation was an indictment of six decades of silence.
For weeks after his death, Tibetan communities across the globe marched and demonstrated. CNN, Radio Free Asia, and others covered it; the U.N. secretary-general’s spokesperson offered condolences, and the U.S. State Department reaffirmed its support for Tibetans. Then, within days, the coverage vanished. No government went beyond boilerplate statements of sympathy.

articles.title: The Potential Mismatch Between Japan and the US on China
articles.full_text:
Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, it is critical for Japan that the United States stays on the same page regarding the challenge from China.
Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae (right) shakes hands with U.S. President Donald Trump during their summit meeting in Tokyo, Japan, Oct. 28, 2025.
As the two most powerful countries in the world today, it is incredibly important that U.S. President Donald Trump will meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on September 24. But before that, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae of Japan is hoping to gain a meeting with Trump during her own visit to the United States for the U.N. General Assembly. 
Both Trump and Takaichi are scheduled to address the General Debate in New York on September 22; as of September 17 “nothing has been decided” regarding a potential meeting, according to Takaichi. 
The China-U.S. summit will have broad implications across a variety of policy areas, and there is no shortage of things for Trump and Xi to talk about. But it will be especially important for Japan, given not just its alliance with the United States, but also its close geographic proximity to China. Takaichi thus hopes to meet with Trump and share Japan’s perspective on China, in order to make sure Japanese interests are considered by its foremost partner.
For Japan, China is a significant threat to its national security that needs to be managed with help from the United States. The security environment in the Indo-Pacific region is under pressure as China continues developing its military capabilities. According to Japan’s defense white paper released last month, “China has been intensifying its activities in the region surrounding Japan [and] extending beyond the so-called first island chain to the second island chain.” 
There are numerous examples of China putting pressure on Japan’s national security and ability to respond. It has upped its coast guard patrols around the island of Taiwan, creating a situation that could threaten Japanese security in the event of a contingency. Japan had to deploy fighters after Chinese and Russian planes were detected in airspace close to the Miyako Strait by Okinawa in June. And Beijing continues to send coast guard ships to patrol inside waters surrounding the disputed Senkaku Islands, claimed by China as the Diaoyu. 
While bilateral Sino-Japanese relations have always vacillated over historical disputes and national security concerns, the current state of the relationship is particularly frigid. It is critical for Japan that the United States – its principal ally and partner – stays on the same page regarding the challenge from China.
The U.S. shares some Japanese concerns about China. Like Tokyo, Washington remains concerned about Chinese assertiveness in the Indo-Pacific region. The U.S., Japan, and other states released a joint statement in August that was critical of China’s unannounced launch of submarine-based long-range ballistic missile. 
The U.S. continues to participate in multilateral military exercises focused on the Indo-Pacific, hosting the Rim of the Pacific exercises in Hawai’i in July, and participating in the May Balikatan exercises with the Philippines. Official references to the Indo-Pacific region are sparser than during the first Trump administration, but the U.S. continues to share its allies’ concerns about Chinese expansion in the region.
At the same time, there are differences between the U.S. and Japan. The conflict in Iran is arguably the Trump administration’s top priority. A report by the Department of Defense inspector general said the conflict was depleting U.S. supplies of important munitions. It has also necessitated the reassignment of the aircraft carrier USS George Washington to the Middle East from the Indo-Pacific region. 
Trump is not a Sinophile, and the U.S. continues to have interests at odds with China’s. But the long-term competition with China may not be as prominent in the mind of Trump, who is bogged down in Iran and related problems. He may be looking for China’s help to ameliorate the worst economic impacts of the war. For example, although the price of oil continues to rise because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, lowered Chinese demand is believed to have a moderating effect on the global oil market. 
To be sure, Washington can talk and chew gum at the same time. And it is not uncommon for allies to have different priorities in diplomacy. This means that the real question is to what extent the U.S. president will take into consideration the equities and viewpoints of allies like Japan. If there is a mismatch in those expectations, it will be critical for the alliance to deal with that friction. 
Two years into his second term, Trump seems to have established a cordial relationship with Takaichi. The broader alliance also remains a firm and important part of national security and diplomacy for both sides. But Japanese wariness about the upcoming Trump-Xi summit and its implications for the Indo-Pacific region are palpable. “With the decline in the U.S. military’s presence in Asia, aren’t China and North Korea taking advantage of this situation?” asked the Yomiuri Shimbun in a September editorial. 
It is difficult to see a major or irreversible rift developing between Washington and Tokyo. But a China-U.S. summit that leaves Japan’s interests out in the cold will be an unneeded challenge for the alliance at a critical time.
Takaichi undoubtedly knows that Trump is a free agent, and that he will do whatever he thinks will “make America great again.” When she meets with Trump ahead of his summit with Xi, her challenge will be to impress upon the U.S. president Japan’s perspective and why it is critical for the Japan-U.S. alliance to continue functioning at a close level. Although the alliance remains strong, a failure to coordinate could lead to friction in this relationship despite its importance to both Washington and Tokyo.
